title: Nintendo Platforming Foundations
blurb: Nintendo EAD's own console-defining leap into 3D, joined by Rare's run of technically dazzling platformers built for the same hardware.
games: The launch title that invented the 3D platformer template almost overnight, with Europe following about nine months after Japan and North America's 1996 debut.
A collectathon that pushed the N64's texture and draw-distance limits further than almost anything before it, released the same year worldwide.
A larger, more interconnected sequel with sprawling worlds that load without a break, released across all three regions in 2000.
A five-character collectathon so item-dense it shipped with its own Expansion Pak requirement, released the same year worldwide.
A storybook-styled platformer built around Yoshi's fruit-eating and melody collecting, with a distinctly gentler difficulty curve than its SNES predecessor.
A frantic side-scrolling shake-em-up from Treasure — one of the platform's more unusual releases, and one that never received a European release at all.
An inventive, underappreciated platformer from the studio that would later create the Infamous series, built around a robot juggling amusement-park guests.
A crude-humor platformer arriving very late in the N64's life, released across all three regions in 2001 just before the system's twilight.
Kirby's only N64 outing, introducing power-combining abilities — released in Japan and North America but never given a European cartridge release.

title: Action & Adventure
blurb: Ocarina of Time redefined 3D action-adventure almost on arrival, in a chapter that also holds Rare's most structurally inventive N64 work.
games: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Widely cited as one of the most influential games ever made, introducing Z-targeting and a day-night cycle — Europe's release followed Japan and North America by a matter of weeks.
The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
A darker, three-day-loop sequel reusing Ocarina's engine and character models, released across all three regions in 2000.
A demolition-puzzle game about clearing a path for a runaway nuclear missile transport, released the same year worldwide.
An open-world alien-invasion adventure from the studio that would soon become Rockstar North, released in North America and Europe with no Japanese release.
A run-and-gun/adventure hybrid with a squad of three playable characters, released across all three regions in 1999.
A physics-driven platformer where the player controls an animated glove rolling a ball through each level, released the same year worldwide.
Released in Japan the year before under its long-running Ganbare Goemon branding, this action-adventure kept its Japanese-culture setting largely intact for its Western release.
A body-swapping action-adventure where a robotic hamster possesses the mechanical animals of an abandoned space station, released the same year worldwide.

title: Shooters & FPS
blurb: GoldenEye 007 proved consoles could do first-person shooters on their own terms, in a chapter carrying two of the N64's most-played multiplayer games.
games: The console FPS's true breakout moment, built around a four-player split-screen mode that came together almost as an afterthought — released the same year worldwide.
GoldenEye's spiritual successor, requiring the Expansion Pak for its full experience and pushing the engine further with bots and a Combat Simulator mode.
Released across Europe as Lylat Wars rather than Star Fox 64, reportedly to avoid a trademark conflict — the same rail-shooter under a different regional name.
A ground-up reimagining of the original Doom with new levels and a moodier atmosphere, rather than a straight port — released in North America and Europe with no Japanese release.
An arcade-style Star Wars flight combat game showing off real-time lighting effects, released in North America in late 1998 with Europe and Japan following into early 1999.
A console conversion of id Software's PC shooter sequel, released across North America and Europe in 1999 with no Japanese release.
A heavily censored N64 port of the PC shooter, stripping out blood, nudity and other content to meet Nintendo's policy — released in North America and Europe with no Japanese release.
One of the N64's earliest FPS releases, built around fog-heavy draw-distance limitations that became part of its distinct look, released the same year worldwide.
A more ambitious sequel requiring the Expansion Pak for its highest visual settings, released the same year worldwide.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: The N64's cartridge storage kept this the smallest chapter in the collection — a genuine reflection of how much thinner the console's RPG output was next to its disc-based rivals.
games: A flat-paper art style wrapped around turn-based RPG combat, released in Japan in 2000 with North America and Europe following into 2001.
Released across Europe as Holy Magic Century rather than Quest 64 — one of the platform's clearer EU-exclusive title changes — with all regions releasing in 1998.
Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber

A tactics-RPG hybrid built around real-time troop movement, released in Japan in 1999 and North America in 2000 — it never received a PAL cartridge release at all, with Europe's first legitimate access coming via a 2010 Wii Virtual Console release.
A farming-sim RPG hybrid continuing the series' day-and-season cycle, released in Japan and North America in 1999 with no European release.
One of the last major N64 RPGs, arriving very late in the console's life in North America in early 2001 with Europe following that August — no Japanese release.
A genre-blending RPG mixing turn-based wrestling-style combat with exploration, released across all three regions in 1999.

title: Racing
blurb: Mario Kart 64 and F-Zero X anchor a chapter that also holds an oddity: a Namco-published racer that, unlike almost everything else the company made, never reached Japan at all.
games: The series' 3D debut, translating Super Mario Kart's Mode 7 tracks into fully polygonal circuits — Europe followed Japan and North America's 1996 launch by several months.
A kart racer with an adventure-mode overworld and vehicle-switching between car, plane and hovercraft, released the same year worldwide.
A high-speed sequel trading Mode 7 scaling for a genuinely 3D track engine running at an unusually high frame rate, released the same year worldwide.
A jet-ski racer praised for water physics well ahead of its time, released in Japan and North America in 1996 with Europe following into 1997.
An arcade port built around exaggerated jumps and shortcuts, released in North America and Europe with no Japanese release.
A rally racer emphasizing car damage modeling, released in North America in 1997 with Europe following into 1998.
An unusual case for a Namco arcade franchise: this N64 entry released only in North America and Europe, with no release in Namco's home market of Japan at all.

title: Sports & Extreme
blurb: 1080° Snowboarding and Camelot's Mario sports spin-offs anchor a chapter built around late-90s extreme-sports style as much as competition.
games: A technically striking snowboarding game praised for its physics and terrain deformation, released the same year worldwide.
A full 18-hole golf sim wrapped in Mushroom Kingdom characters, released the same year worldwide.
A tennis game notable for introducing Waluigi to the Mario cast, released the same year worldwide.
An exaggerated, rules-light arcade football conversion, released across North America and Europe the same year despite its distinctly American sport.
A Volkswagen Beetle-themed arcade racer built around wide, secret-filled tracks, released across all three regions in 1999.
An arcade racer conversion that, unusually, reached Europe nearly three months before its North American release — no Japanese release.
A cartoonish snowboarding-kart hybrid that reached the West in 1998 before its Japanese release the following year, an unusual reversal of the platform's typical regional order.

title: Fighting
blurb: Super Smash Bros. debuted here almost as a side project before becoming one of Nintendo's biggest franchises, alongside a chapter full of wrestling and licensed brawlers.
games: The series' debut, built around percentage-based knockback rather than traditional health bars, released in Japan in January 1999 with the West following later that year.
An enhanced N64 port of the arcade fighter adding new characters and combo-training tools, released in North America in 1996 with Europe following into 1997.
A compilation port gathering nearly every character from the series' first three arcade entries onto one cartridge, released in North America in 1996 with Europe following into 1997.

Released in Japan as Fighting Cup, this point-scoring fighter rewarded ring-outs and style over simple knockouts — an unusual case where the Japanese release reportedly followed the West rather than leading it.
A claymation-styled parody fighter released only in North America, with no European or Japanese release.
Widely regarded as one of the best wrestling games ever made, released across North America and Europe in 2000.
A predecessor to No Mercy sharing its acclaimed grapple-based engine, released in Europe in October 1999, days ahead of its North American release, with Japan following nearly a year later.
An exaggerated arcade boxing game built around cartoonish character designs, released in North America and Europe in 1999 with Japan following into 2000.
A wrestling game sharing its engine with the WWF titles under a rival promotion's license, released in North America in October 1998 with Europe following about a month later.

title: Puzzle & Party
blurb: Hudson Soft's Mario Party trilogy anchors a chapter of four-player-focused puzzle and board-game hybrids built around the N64's four controller ports.
games: The series debut built entirely around its four controller ports, released in Japan and North America in 1998 with Europe following into 1999.
A sequel adding costumed characters and more varied minigame boards, released in Japan and North America in 1999 with Europe following into 2000.
The trilogy's closer, adding a story mode and duel-format minigames, released in Japan and North America in 2000 with Europe following into 2001.
A 3D reinvention of the series mixing platforming stages with the traditional multiplayer arena battles, released in North America and Japan in 1997 with Europe following into 1998.
A more action-adventure-focused spin-off dropping the traditional battle-arena multiplayer in favor of a linear campaign, released across all three regions around 1998–1999.
A Pokémon-themed reskin of Tetris Attack's puzzle engine, released the same year worldwide.
An unusual spherical take on Tetris built around clearing tiles from a rotating 3D globe, released in North America in 1997 with Europe following into 1998.
A physics-driven puzzle game about managing rising water on a deforming 3D landscape, released across all three regions in 1998.

title: Simulation & Strategy
blurb: Pokémon Snap and Pokémon Stadium anchor a chapter that also holds SimCity's own sequel — a title that, unusually, never left Japan on this platform at all.
games: A rail-shooter-styled photography game built around capturing wild Pokémon on camera, released in Japan and North America in 1999 with Europe following into 2000.
A 3D battle simulator letting players import their Game Boy Pokémon into fully rendered arena fights, released the same year across North America and Europe.
A sequel adding support for the Gold and Silver generation, released in Japan in 2000 with North America and Europe following into 2001.
A city-building sequel adding mini-games and disaster events on top of the original's simulation — a Japan-exclusive N64 release that never reached the West on this platform at all.
A console conversion of the PC real-time strategy landmark, released across North America and Europe in 1999 with no Japanese release.
A turn-based artillery-strategy hit ported to N64, released in Europe in December 1999 with North America following into early 2000 — no Japanese release.
A third-person shooter starring green plastic toy soldiers, released across North America and Europe in 1999 with no Japanese release.

title: Licensed, Movie & TV Tie-ins
blurb: LucasArts' pair of Star Wars N64 exclusives anchor a chapter of largely well-regarded licensed titles, including two spy-franchise shooters riding GoldenEye's success.
games: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire
An original Star Wars story filling the gap between The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, released the same year worldwide.
A podracing game built to show off the N64's speed-sensation rendering, released the same year worldwide alongside the film it was based on.
A well-regarded web-slinging action game, released in North America and Europe in 2001 with no Japanese release.
A crude-humor first-person shooter based on the animated series, released in North America in 1998 with Europe following into 1999.

A GoldenEye-styled Bond FPS built by the same genre lineage rather than the same studio, released in North America in October 2000 with Europe following that December — no Japanese release, as with the platform's other Bond titles.
Batman Beyond: Return of the Joker
An animated-series tie-in platformer, released in North America in late 2000 with Europe following in January 2001 — no Japanese release.
Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue
A well-received platformer built around the film's cast, released the same year worldwide.
A stealth-action title based on the 1996 film, released across North America and Europe in 1998 with no Japanese release.

An N64-specific port of the giant-monster arcade brawler, built by a different studio than the PlayStation version, released in North America in September 1997 with Europe following that December — no Japanese release.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: A trio of celebrated Japan-exclusive titles anchors this chapter — games the West only ever got to experience through much later re-releases on entirely different hardware.
games: A rail-shooter/action hybrid from Treasure, released only in Japan — its first official Western release came seven years later via Wii Virtual Console.
A robot-battling RPG hybrid that launched a small franchise, Japan-exclusive on N64; the series wouldn't reach the West until later Game Boy Advance and GameCube entries.
The original life-sim that would become Animal Crossing, Japan-exclusive on N64 — its Western debut came via an enhanced GameCube port in 2002 (NA) and 2004 (EU).
A 3D revival of the NES original blending motocross racing with a track-editor mode, released in North America and Japan in 2000 with Europe following into 2001.
An offbeat platformer starring a tongue-grappling chameleon, released in Japan and North America in 1997 with Europe following into 1998.
A rolling-ball arena platformer released in North America in 1998 with Europe following into 1999 — no Japanese release.
A story-driven sequel with a notably darker tone than the original, released in Japan and North America in 1999–2000 with no European release.
A vehicular-combat game with a 1970s setting, released in North America and Europe in 1999 with no Japanese release.
An unusual bee-themed flight-combat shooter, released across all three regions in late 1998.

title: Arcade Ports & Multiplayer Curios
blurb: The largest chapter in the collection, gathering Midway's arcade conversions alongside a run of licensed and original multiplayer-focused racers and shooters.
games: An early arcade racing port and one of the N64's launch-window titles, released in North America in 1996 with Europe following into 1997 — no Japanese release.
A stunt-jump-heavy arcade racing sequel, released across North America and Europe in 1998 with no Japanese release.
A high-speed anti-gravity racer from a British studio, released across all three regions in 1997.
A basketball sim built exclusively for the North American market, with no European or Japanese release.
An arcade-style hockey game released in North America in late 1996 with Europe following into 1997 — Japan's release trailed by over a year.
A British-developed miniature-vehicle racer released across all three regions in 1999.
A wisecracking platformer starring a gecko television addict, released across North America and Europe in 1998 with no Japanese release.
Released in Europe the year before as Bust-A-Move 3 DX, this puzzle game reached Europe well ahead of its own Japanese (as Puzzle Bobble 64) and North American releases.
An exaggerated arcade basketball conversion, released in North America in early 1997 with Europe following that September — no Japanese release.
Released in Japan as Super Speed Race 64 through a different publisher, this supercar racer reached North America and Europe first, with Japan following about six months later.
A futuristic sequel to the Rush arcade series, released across North America and Europe in 2000 with no Japanese release.
A sequel continuing the giant-monster arcade brawler formula, released across North America and Europe in 1999 with no Japanese release.
